summary: Tenths build on earlier work with fractions such as halves and quarters: dividing ONE whole into ten equal parts, and the bridge toward decimal place value. The load-bearing ideas are that ten equal tenths recompose exactly one whole (10/10 = 1), that each tenth is small because it takes ten of them to rebuild the whole, and that 3/10 is the same as 3÷10 (three wholes shared among ten). Partitioned strips, length-based number lines, and sharing models let counting in tenths land cleanly at one whole rather than drifting into 'ten'.
misconceptions: Whole-number bias — reads ten-tenths as 'ten', or thinks a tenth is big 'because 10 is a big number'
Larger denominator = larger part (a tenth 'bigger than a half because 10 > 2')
Accepts any ten pieces as tenths, ignoring that the parts must be equal
Sees no connection between 3/10 and 3÷10 ('3 ÷ 10 can't be done, 3 is smaller than 10')
Thinks a tenth of a large whole and a tenth of a small whole are the same size

activities.title: Collect the tenths back into one whole
steps: Start with a single whole bar or strip and partition it into ten equal segments.
Collect the segments one at a time while counting aloud: one-tenth, two-tenths, three-tenths … up to ten-tenths.
At the tenth count, reassemble the ten segments end-to-end against the original whole and check that they match exactly, labelling the result '10/10 = 1 whole'.
Lay a piece covering exactly five tenths over one half of the whole and confirm that 5/10 = 1/2, so a single tenth is plainly far smaller than a half.
activities.insight: Ten equal tenths put back together remake exactly one whole, so 10/10 = 1 (not 'ten'), and each tenth is small because it takes ten of them to rebuild the whole — far smaller than a half.

activities.title: Share three wholes among ten to see 3/10 = 3÷10
steps: Set out three identical whole bars and ten plates (or ten places) to share them among.
Partition each whole into tenths and deal the tenths out equally, one at a time, until each of the ten places has received the same amount.
State how much each place received (three tenths) and write the sharing as 3 ÷ 10 = 3/10.
Discuss why this works even though 3 is smaller than 10: you share the three wholes into smaller pieces rather than giving whole bars each.
activities.insight: A fraction such as 3/10 is the result of sharing three wholes equally among ten, so 3/10 = 3÷10; dividing by a number larger than the dividend is possible and gives a fraction less than one.

activities.title: Equal parts only, and the same whole
steps: Compare a whole split into ten EQUAL pieces with a whole split into ten UNEQUAL pieces.
Decide which one shows tenths and explain why (the ten parts must be the same size).
Check by trying to recompose each set back into the whole and noticing which one tiles the whole with matching equal pieces.

Then compare a tenth of a small whole bar with a tenth of a larger whole bar, keeping both wholes visible, and describe how the two tenths differ in physical size even though both are called 'a tenth'.
activities.insight: Only ten EQUAL parts of one whole count as tenths; and because a tenth is defined relative to its whole, the physical piece that is a tenth of a larger whole is larger than a tenth of a smaller whole when both wholes are shown, though both pieces share the name 'a tenth' and name the same fraction of their own whole.

activities.title: Place and name tenths on a number line
steps: Use a 0-to-1 number line marked in tenths.
Count up and down the line in tenths, naming each mark.
Place given tenths (for example 3/10) at the correct point and identify which point equals one half (5/10).
Fill in missing values such as 'ten-tenths = __' and justify with the recomposition idea rather than by counting ticks.
activities.insight: Tenths are single numbers with a fixed position and magnitude between 0 and 1, with 10/10 sitting exactly at one and 5/10 exactly at one half.

checkQuestion: A chocolate bar is one whole. It is snapped into ten equal pieces. I eat the pieces one at a time and count: one-tenth, two-tenths, three-tenths… When I have eaten all of them, I have eaten ten-tenths. What number does ten-tenths equal, and why? And is each single piece bigger or smaller than a half — how do you know?
checkAnswer: Ten-tenths equals 1 (one whole), because ten equal tenths put back together make the whole bar again. Each tenth is much smaller than a half, because it takes ten tenths to make a whole but only two halves — so a tenth is far smaller (five tenths make one half).
